input:
Feedback control is a fundamental idea in process engineering, and a clear way to understand it is the level loop, in which the level of liquid in a process vessel is held at its desired value by adjusting a flow. The loop has several parts, worked through in turn: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback that ties the arrangement together.

The sensor measures the level in the vessel and converts the measurement into a signal passed to the rest of the system. The reading is the loop's only source of information about the level: everything the loop does is done in response to the reading rather than the level itself, so a faulty reading makes the rest of the loop act faithfully on incorrect information.

The controller receives the reading and compares it with the set point, the level the vessel is intended to maintain. The difference between set point and reading is the error, and the controller uses it to work out the correction required, producing an instruction whose size and direction depend on that error.

The final element puts the controller's instruction into practice, and in a level loop it is typically a valve on a line entering or leaving the vessel. When the valve moves, the flow changes; when the flow changes, the level changes; and the changed level is picked up by the sensor, closing the loop.

Finally, the sign of the feedback in a level loop is negative, and this is what makes the arrangement work as a regulator. If the level rises above the set point, the correction acts to bring it down again, and if it falls, the correction acts to raise it, so the loop continually opposes the disturbance that moved it. Were the sign positive instead, the loop would push the level ever further from the set point, either filling the vessel or emptying it altogether.
target:
A level loop holds the level in a process vessel at its set point by acting on a stream entering or leaving the vessel. The loop has four parts, taken in order: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback that joins them.

The sensor measures the level and reports it to the controller as a signal. Level is the height of liquid in the vessel, and the reading is the loop's only knowledge of it: every later part acts on the reading, not on the level itself, so a faulty reading drives correct hardware to a wrong action.

The controller compares the reading with the set point and decides the correction. Set point is the level the vessel is to hold. The comparison gives an error, the difference between set point and reading, and the controller turns the error into an instruction whose size and direction follow from it.

The final element carries out the instruction, and in a level loop it is a valve on an inlet or outlet line. The valve changes the flow, the flow changes the level, and the sensor reads the changed level. Measurement, decision and action follow one another continuously while the vessel runs, and the loop is closed.

The sign of the feedback is negative. A rise in level above the set point produces a correction that lowers the level, and a fall produces a correction that raises it, so the loop opposes the disturbance that moved it. Feedback of the opposite sign would drive the level away from the set point and empty or fill the vessel. Negative sign is what makes the arrangement a regulator rather than an amplifier of error.
